summary: Atypical antipsychotic reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and persistent suicidality. Highly effective but requires strict blood monitoring due to risk of severe neutropenia, myocarditis, seizures, and major metabolic side effects.
description: Clozapine is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic used when at least two other antipsychotics have failed or when someone with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder has ongoing suicidal thoughts or behaviors. It can dramatically reduce psychotic symptoms and suicidality when other medications haven’t worked, but it carries serious risks: severe neutropenia (dangerously low white blood cells), myocarditis and cardiomyopathy, seizures, severe constipation and bowel blockage, weight gain, diabetes, and high cholesterol. Because of these risks, clozapine requires regular blood tests (ANC monitoring), slow dose titration, and careful monitoring for side effects. It is not a first-line antipsychotic and should be managed by a specialist familiar with its use.
patient_summary:
Clozapine is a powerful antipsychotic used when other medications for schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder haven’t worked, or when someone remains very suicidal despite treatment. It can be life-changing—reducing voices, paranoia, and suicidal thoughts—but it also has serious risks.

The biggest is a dangerous drop in white blood cells (severe neutropenia), which can lead to life-threatening infections. Because of this, you must get regular blood tests to stay on clozapine. It can also cause heart inflammation (myocarditis), seizures, very bad constipation or bowel blockage, major weight gain, high blood sugar, and high cholesterol.

Clozapine is usually started at a very low dose and increased slowly to reduce side effects like dizziness, low blood pressure, and sedation. It should only be used under close medical supervision, and never stopped suddenly without talking to your prescriber.

primary.context: Reserved for severely ill patients with schizophrenia who have not responded adequately to at least two other antipsychotics at appropriate doses and durations.
Indicated to reduce recurrent suicidal behavior in patients with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who are at chronic risk.

secondary.context: Occasionally used for severe agitation or psychosis in dementia when other treatments fail, but carries increased mortality risk and is NOT approved for dementia-related psychosis.

off_label.context: Used off-label in treatment-resistant bipolar disorder, particularly with severe mania or mixed features not responding to standard mood stabilizers and antipsychotics.
Very low doses may be used off-label for Parkinson disease psychosis when other options fail, due to low risk of motor side effects.

therapeutic_response.display: Psychiatric benefit often begins within 1–2 weeks, with full effects over several weeks to months due to slow titration.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Feeling tired, sleepy, or ‘drugged’ is common, especially at the start and after dose increases. Dosing more at bedtime and slow titration can help. Avoid driving until you know how clozapine affects you.
You may feel lightheaded when standing up. Stand slowly, stay hydrated, and report any fainting episodes. This risk is highest in the first few weeks or after dose changes.
Excess saliva and drooling, especially at night, can be embarrassing and bothersome. Simple strategies (towel on pillow, mouth position) and medications can sometimes reduce it.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Very common (GI hypomotility reported in up to ~30%)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Bowel movements may slow or stop. This is not just uncomfortable—it can become dangerous. You’ll likely need a daily bowel regimen (fiber, fluids, laxatives). Report any severe abdominal pain or no bowel movement for several days immediately.

Many people gain significant weight and see increases in cholesterol and blood sugar. Diet, exercise, and regular lab monitoring are essential. Sometimes additional medications are needed for diabetes or cholesterol.
A faster heartbeat is common, especially early on. Severe palpitations, chest pain, or shortness of breath need urgent evaluation to rule out myocarditis or other heart problems.

Mild, short-lived fever can occur but may also signal serious problems like infection, myocarditis, or low white blood cells. Any fever on clozapine should be taken seriously and discussed with your care team.

serious_risks.risk: Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis: Very low white blood cells leading to life-threatening infections. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or feeling very unwell.
Myocarditis and cardiomyopathy: Heart inflammation or damage causing chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, fatigue, or swelling.
Seizures, status epilepticus, or myoclonus: Sudden convulsions or jerking movements. Risk increases with higher doses or rapid titration.

Severe gastrointestinal hypomotility: Ileus, bowel obstruction, megacolon, intestinal ischemia, perforation, and peritonitis—presenting with severe abdominal pain, bloating, vomiting, or no bowel movements.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Rare but life-threatening reaction with high fever, muscle rigidity (sometimes less obvious with clozapine), confusion, and autonomic instability.
Severe liver injury: Marked rise in liver enzymes, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, or abdominal pain.
Venous thromboembolism: Blood clots in legs (DVT) or lungs (PE) causing leg swelling, chest pain, or sudden shortness of breath.
Severe arrhythmias and QTc prolongation: Irregular heartbeat, fainting, or sudden cardiac death in high-risk patients.
Severe temperature dysregulation: Heatstroke in hot weather or hypothermia (dangerously low body temperature) in cold environments.
Agranulocytosis or severe infections: Sepsis, pneumonia, and other serious infections requiring hospitalization.

safety.black_box_warning: Severe neutropenia (very low neutrophils) can lead to life-threatening infections and death. Clozapine requires regular ANC monitoring before and during treatment. Clozapine also increases mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis and is NOT approved for this use.

contraindications.contraindication: Serious hypersensitivity reaction to clozapine (eg, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, vasculitis, photosensitivity)
History of clozapine-induced agranulocytosis or severe neutropenia
Baseline ANC <1,500/mm³ in general population (or <1,000/mm³ in patients with Duffy-null associated neutrophil count)
Active hepatic disease with jaundice, nausea, or anorexia; progressive hepatic failure
Severe cardiac disease (eg, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, recent serious arrhythmia) unless cleared by cardiology
Paralytic ileus or serious bowel obstruction
Concomitant use of other drugs that significantly suppress bone marrow (per Canadian labeling)

precautions: Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis: Can occur at any time, but risk is highest in the first 6 months. Any fever, sore throat, or flu-like symptoms require urgent evaluation.
Myocarditis and cardiomyopathy: Can present with fatigue, chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, or unexplained fever—especially in the first 1–2 months.
Seizures: Risk increases with higher doses and rapid titration. Caution in people with seizure history, brain injury, or on other seizure-threshold-lowering drugs.
Severe constipation and bowel blockage: Clozapine can slow the gut so much that life-threatening bowel obstruction, perforation, or paralytic ileus can occur.
Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: Sudden drops in blood pressure when standing can lead to falls, especially early in treatment or with dose increases.
Metabolic syndrome: High risk of significant weight gain, high cholesterol, and diabetes—these need active monitoring and management.
Increased mortality in dementia: In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics increase the risk of death and stroke. Clozapine is not approved for this group.
Temperature dysregulation: Both fever and hypothermia have been reported; both require evaluation.
Venous thromboembolism: Blood clots in the legs or lungs (DVT/PE) have been reported, sometimes fatal.

interactions.mechanism: Smoking induces CYP1A2 and can lower clozapine levels; stopping smoking can significantly increase levels and toxicity.
interactions.action: Tell your prescriber about any change in smoking (starting, stopping, more, or less). Doses often need to be reduced 30–40% after quitting smoking and adjusted upward if you start smoking again.

interactions.mechanism: Can greatly increase clozapine levels, raising risk of seizures, sedation, low blood pressure, and myocarditis.
interactions.action: Avoid if possible. If needed, clozapine dose usually must be reduced substantially and levels/side effects monitored closely.

interactions.interactant: Strong CYP3A4 Inhibitors (eg, ketoconazole, certain HIV meds, some macrolide antibiotics)
interactions.mechanism: Increase clozapine concentrations and toxicity risk.
interactions.action: Use alternatives if possible. If unavoidable, use lower clozapine doses with careful monitoring.

interactions.interactant: CYP Inducers (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John’s wort)
interactions.mechanism: May lower clozapine levels and effectiveness; carbamazepine also adds bone marrow suppression risk.
interactions.action: Avoid carbamazepine and other bone-marrow-suppressing drugs. If other inducers are needed, expect possible loss of effect and discuss alternatives.

interactions.interactant: Other Bone Marrow–Suppressing Drugs (eg, certain chemotherapies, carbamazepine, some antithyroid drugs)
interactions.mechanism: Additive risk of severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis.
interactions.action: Generally avoid combining. If unavoidable (eg, cancer treatment), coordinate closely with hematology/oncology and intensify blood count monitoring.

interactions.interactant: Benzodiazepines or Other Sedatives (eg, lorazepam, opioids, alcohol, antihistamines, sleep meds)
interactions.mechanism: Increased sedation, low blood pressure, breathing problems, and fall risk. Rare reports of collapse or respiratory compromise with rapid clozapine plus benzodiazepine titration.
interactions.action: Use cautiously at lowest effective doses, especially when starting or raising clozapine. Avoid alcohol. Monitor for excessive sedation or breathing problems.

interactions.interactant: Anticholinergic Drugs (eg, some antidepressants, antihistamines, bladder meds, other antipsychotics)
interactions.mechanism: Additive constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion, and possible bowel obstruction.
interactions.action: Minimize additional anticholinergic meds when possible and use a proactive bowel regimen. Monitor for urinary retention and confusion.

interactions.interactant: QT-Prolonging Medications (eg, some antiarrhythmics, macrolide antibiotics, fluoroquinolones, some antidepressants)
interactions.mechanism: Additive QTc prolongation and potential torsades de pointes in high-risk patients.
interactions.action: Check baseline ECG and electrolytes in at-risk patients. Avoid combining multiple QT-prolonging drugs whenever possible.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Absolute neutrophil count (ANC): Mandatory baseline and ongoing ANC monitoring (typically weekly for 6 months, then every 2 weeks for 6 months, then monthly if stable). Different thresholds apply for people with Duffy-null associated neutrophil counts.
Vital signs: Blood pressure (including orthostatic), heart rate, temperature at baseline and regularly—especially in the first few weeks and after dose increases.

Myocarditis/cardiomyopathy monitoring: Watch for chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, fatigue, unexplained fever, and resting tachycardia. Some clinicians monitor CRP and troponin weekly for the first 4–6 weeks.
Metabolic monitoring: Weight/BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and lipid panel at baseline, around 3–4 months after starting, then at least annually (more often if abnormal).
Bowel function: Ask about bowel movements at every visit; track frequency, consistency, and associated symptoms. Consider prophylactic laxatives.
Liver and kidney function: Periodic liver enzymes and renal function tests, especially in those with preexisting disease or on other hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic drugs.
Neurologic status: Monitor for seizures, myoclonus, confusion, delirium, or new movement symptoms. Consider EEG if clinically indicated or at higher doses.
ECG: Baseline in those with cardiac risk factors or on other QT-prolonging drugs; repeat if symptoms occur or if risk factors change.
Adherence and side effects: At every visit, assess how consistently clozapine is taken, barriers to adherence (labs, side effects, logistics), and emerging adverse effects.
Smoking status and drug interactions: Regularly review tobacco use and new medications to anticipate changes in clozapine levels and risks.

special_populations.pregnancy: Clozapine crosses the placenta. Available data on birth defects are limited and mixed. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics, including clozapine, can cause withdrawal or movement symptoms in newborns (breathing problems, feeding issues, stiffness or floppiness). Clozapine also raises the risk of weight gain and diabetes in the pregnant parent, which can affect pregnancy outcomes. If a patient is stable on clozapine before pregnancy and alternatives are not likely to work, many guidelines support continuing it at the lowest effective dose with close monitoring, rather than stopping and risking severe relapse.
special_populations.lactation: Clozapine passes into breast milk and has been associated with sedation and at least one case of suspected agranulocytosis in a breastfed infant. Because of the potential for serious adverse effects (sedation, poor feeding, blood problems), clozapine is generally not recommended while breastfeeding. If used, the baby should be monitored very closely by pediatrics.
special_populations.pediatric: Clozapine is used in children and adolescents only for severe, treatment-resistant schizophrenia and usually under specialist care. Dosing is weight-based and titrated slowly. Children may be at higher risk of some side effects (eg, metabolic problems, movement symptoms), and they still require full ANC monitoring.
special_populations.geriatric: Older adults are more sensitive to clozapine’s side effects—especially low blood pressure, sedation, falls, constipation, confusion, and heart issues. Start at very low doses, increase very slowly, and use the smallest effective dose. Antipsychotics in general are associated with increased stroke and mortality risk in older adults with dementia.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Kidney impairment may increase clozapine exposure. Start at low doses, titrate slowly, and monitor for side effects. Dose reductions may be needed in significant kidney impairment.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Liver disease can increase clozapine levels. Use lower starting doses, slower titration, and regular monitoring of liver tests. Stop and evaluate if there are signs of liver injury (jaundice, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant pain).

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally; bioavailability is moderate and not significantly affected by food.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: About 2–3 hours after an oral dose (tablets or ODT).
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Average ~12 hours (range 4–66 hours), longer at higher doses or with metabolic inhibition.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic via CYP1A2 (major), CYP3A4 and CYP2C19/2D6 (minor) to active and inactive metabolites (eg, norclozapine).
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily in urine (about 50%) and feces (about 30%) as metabolites; very little unchanged drug is excreted.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food does not meaningfully change overall absorption.

dosing.titration: Clozapine dosing is highly individualized. It is always started low and increased slowly to reduce serious side effects like low blood pressure, myocarditis, and seizures. A psychiatry specialist should direct dosing.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Clozapine should almost never be stopped suddenly unless there is a life-threatening reaction (eg, severe neutropenia, myocarditis). Abrupt discontinuation can cause rapid return of psychosis, severe withdrawal symptoms, and even catatonia.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Clozapine is a highly specialized antipsychotic used when standard treatments for schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder have not worked or when there is ongoing suicidal risk. Because of its serious side effects, it’s typically reserved for people who have failed at least two other antipsychotics.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Treatment-resistant schizophrenia}: Severe symptoms that persist despite adequate trials of at least two other antipsychotics.
{link:condition:schizoaffective-disorder:Schizoaffective disorder with suicidality}: Reduces the risk of suicidal behavior in people judged to be at chronic risk.
Severe aggression, agitation, or self-harm risk: When other medications and behavioral strategies have failed and the person is at risk of harming themselves or others.
Parkinson disease psychosis (off-label): Very low doses may be used when safer options fail and psychosis is severely impairing.

Severe or refractory dementia-related psychosis (off-label): Sometimes used short-term for extreme agitation or psychosis when non-drug and safer drug options have failed, but carries increased stroke and mortality risk.
off_label: Treatment-resistant bipolar disorder (acute mania or mixed states)
Severe aggression or self-injurious behavior in certain neurodevelopmental conditions (specialist use)
Refractory psychosis in other severe mood or psychotic disorders

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: The voices got quieter first, then less mean.
I still heard some things, but they bothered me less.
Paranoia dialed down—I wasn’t constantly scanning the room.
The first week, I felt like I’d taken a strong sleeping pill.
Standing up too fast made me feel lightheaded.
I slept 10–12 hours a night at first.
items.note: Sedation and low blood pressure are common early on, especially during dose increases. They often improve over time but can remain an issue for some people.

quotes: I was hungrier all the time and gained weight quickly.
My blood sugar and cholesterol started creeping up.
I felt bloated and constipated if I didn’t stay on top of fiber and fluids.
items.note: Weight gain, increased appetite, constipation, and changes in blood sugar and cholesterol are common and need active management.

quotes: I drool on my pillow at night now—it’s embarrassing.
My mouth can be dry during the day but I still drool at night.
Sometimes I feel a bit shaky or twitchy when the dose goes up.
items.note: Sialorrhea (drooling), constipation, and mild movement changes (like myoclonus) can occur and should be discussed with your prescriber.

quotes: The blood tests are annoying, but I got used to the routine.
I actually feel safer knowing they’re checking my white blood cell count.
Missing a lab can mean they hold my meds, so I set lots of reminders.
items.note: Regular blood work (ANC checks) is mandatory to stay on clozapine. Many people find the structure helpful once it becomes routine.

sections.intro: Experiences vary, but these are common themes people report when starting and staying on clozapine:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Clozapine does not work instantly. It’s titrated slowly to reduce side effects, so improvements build over weeks.
key_points: First few days: Sedation, dizziness, and low blood pressure are often more noticeable than symptom improvement.
1–2 weeks: Some people notice early changes in sleep, anxiety, or intensity of voices.
4–8 weeks: Clearer reductions in hallucinations, paranoia, and disorganization for many patients as dose reaches therapeutic range.
Beyond 8 weeks: Continued fine-tuning of dose; benefits on suicidality, aggression, and overall functioning often become more apparent over time.
Duration: Clozapine is a long-term maintenance treatment. Stopping it abruptly can lead to rapid relapse and serious withdrawal symptoms.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: For people with schizophrenia who have not responded to at least two other antipsychotics, clozapine is often the only medication with a meaningful chance of success. Across studies, about one-third to more than half of these ‘treatment-resistant’ patients show major improvement in psychotic symptoms on clozapine. It is also the only antipsychotic specifically approved to reduce suicidal behavior in schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder.
sections.comparison: Much higher than response rates seen when simply trying more of the same antipsychotics that have already failed.
sections.clinical_details: Clinical trials and long-term observational cohorts show that clozapine outperforms other antipsychotics in patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, with substantially higher response rates and lower rates of rehospitalization and suicide. Clozapine’s benefits come at the cost of a more complex safety profile, requiring intensive monitoring (particularly ANC checks) and careful management of metabolic and cardiovascular risks.

citation.title: Clozapine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia and suicidality
citation.journal: Various (eg, British Journal of Psychiatry, American Journal of Psychiatry, Schizophrenia Bulletin)

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Clozapine can cause life-threatening drops in white blood cells, serious heart inflammation, seizures, and severe bowel problems. Regular blood tests and close monitoring are not optional—they are essential.
sections.black_box: Severe neutropenia (very low neutrophils) can lead to life-threatening infections and death. Clozapine requires regular ANC monitoring before and during treatment. Clozapine also increases mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis and is NOT approved for this use.
other: Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis: Can occur at any time, but risk is highest in the first 6 months. Any fever, sore throat, or flu-like symptoms require urgent evaluation.
Myocarditis and cardiomyopathy: Can present with fatigue, chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, or unexplained fever—especially in the first 1–2 months.
Seizures: Risk increases with higher doses and rapid titration. Caution in people with seizure history, brain injury, or on other seizure-threshold-lowering drugs.
Severe constipation and bowel blockage: Clozapine can slow the gut so much that life-threatening bowel obstruction, perforation, or paralytic ileus can occur.
Orthostatic hypotension and syncope: Sudden drops in blood pressure when standing can lead to falls, especially early in treatment or with dose increases.
Metabolic syndrome: High risk of significant weight gain, high cholesterol, and diabetes—these need active monitoring and management.
Increased mortality in dementia: In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics increase the risk of death and stroke. Clozapine is not approved for this group.
Temperature dysregulation: Both fever and hypothermia have been reported; both require evaluation.
Venous thromboembolism: Blood clots in the legs or lungs (DVT/PE) have been reported, sometimes fatal.
patient_counseling: You must keep all blood test appointments. Missing labs can lead to your pharmacy stopping clozapine and may put you at risk.
Call your doctor or seek urgent care immediately if you get fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, flu-like symptoms, chest pain, shortness of breath, fast heartbeat, or feel unusually weak.
Report new or severe constipation, abdominal pain, vomiting, or a swollen belly right away—they can be emergencies on clozapine.
Change positions slowly (lying → sitting → standing) to reduce dizziness and fainting.
Tell your team if you start or stop smoking—this can change clozapine levels in your blood.
Do not stop clozapine suddenly unless your doctor tells you to. Abrupt stopping can cause severe rebound psychosis, withdrawal, or catatonia.
Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs; they can worsen sedation, blood pressure drops, and seizure risk.
Keep an up-to-date medication list and show it to every provider—many drugs interact with clozapine or can also lower white blood cells.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common side effects include sedation, dizziness, drooling, constipation, weight gain, and metabolic changes. Serious but less common risks include severe neutropenia, myocarditis, seizures, bowel obstruction, and blood clots.

Increased saliva and drooling, especially at night
Constipation (can be severe or dangerous if untreated)
Changes in blood sugar and cholesterol (diabetes and high cholesterol)
Fast heartbeat and low blood pressure
Fever, flu-like symptoms, or frequent infections (could signal low white blood cells)

sections.intro: Clozapine levels are strongly affected by smoking, certain antibiotics, antifungals, anticonvulsants, and other psych meds. Many medications also add to its side effects or bone marrow risks.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Clozapine should almost never be stopped suddenly unless there is a life-threatening reaction (eg, severe neutropenia, myocarditis). Abrupt discontinuation can cause rapid return of psychosis, severe withdrawal symptoms, and even catatonia.
key_points: Planned discontinuation should be gradual over weeks to months, with close monitoring for relapse of psychosis, mood changes, or withdrawal.
Common withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, insomnia, headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, restlessness, and flu-like feelings.
Rebound psychosis or cholinergic rebound (sweating, diarrhea, nausea) can occur if the dose is dropped too quickly.
In stable patients, many experts recommend tapering by about 10% of the dose every 1–2 weeks, with slower reductions at lower doses.

If clozapine needs to be stopped urgently due to serious side effects (eg, severe neutropenia or myocarditis), hospitalization and intensive monitoring are often needed. Alternative antipsychotics are usually started promptly.
If clozapine is interrupted for more than 2 days, it must be restarted at 12.5 mg once or twice daily and titrated again to reduce risk of low blood pressure and cardiac events.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Clozapine dosing is highly individualized. It is always started low and increased slowly to reduce serious side effects like low blood pressure, myocarditis, and seizures. A psychiatry specialist should direct dosing.

adult.schizophrenia_initial: 12.5 mg once or twice daily on day 1, then 25–50 mg/day in divided doses on subsequent days as tolerated.
adult.schizophrenia_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg/day no more often than once daily to a target of 300–450 mg/day by the end of 2 weeks.
adult.schizophrenia_typical: Common effective range is 300–600 mg/day in 1–2 divided doses; some patients need higher or lower doses.
adult.schizophrenia_max: 900 mg/day (higher doses carry increased seizure risk and require close monitoring).
adult.reinitiation: If therapy is interrupted ≥2 days, restart at 12.5 mg once or twice daily and retitrate.
adult.bipolar_off_label: Typical acute mania doses are within similar ranges (eg, 100–300 mg/day, up to ~550 mg/day) with slow titration.
adult.elderly: Start 12.5 mg once daily for 3 days, then 25 mg once daily for 3 days as tolerated. Increase by 12.5–25 mg every 3 days, usually not exceeding 300–400 mg/day. Go slower and use lower maximum doses.
adult.renal: eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m²: No formal adjustment; monitor closely. eGFR <60 or on dialysis: Start at low end of dosing range, titrate more slowly, and monitor for side effects.
adult.hepatic: No formal dosage table, but dose reduction and slower titration are recommended in significant hepatic impairment. Avoid or use extreme caution in active or progressive liver disease.
adult.duffy_null_neutrophil: Two baseline ANC measurements are recommended. Do not start if ANC <1,000/mm³. Monitoring schedule differs slightly from general population.

sections.simple_explanation: Clozapine is started at a very low dose (usually 12.5 mg) and increased slowly over days to weeks. Most people take it twice a day, with more of the dose at night to reduce daytime sedation. The final dose depends on how well symptoms respond and how well your body tolerates the medicine. Regular blood tests and medical check-ins are part of the treatment.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Clozapine may be continued in pregnancy or breastfeeding when benefits clearly outweigh risks, but it is not usually started for the first time during pregnancy unless absolutely necessary. Decisions should involve shared decision-making with psychiatry and obstetrics.
sections.pregnancy: Clozapine crosses the placenta. Available data on birth defects are limited and mixed. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics, including clozapine, can cause withdrawal or movement symptoms in newborns (breathing problems, feeding issues, stiffness or floppiness). Clozapine also raises the risk of weight gain and diabetes in the pregnant parent, which can affect pregnancy outcomes. If a patient is stable on clozapine before pregnancy and alternatives are not likely to work, many guidelines support continuing it at the lowest effective dose with close monitoring, rather than stopping and risking severe relapse.
sections.lactation: Clozapine passes into breast milk and has been associated with sedation and at least one case of suspected agranulocytosis in a breastfed infant. Because of the potential for serious adverse effects (sedation, poor feeding, blood problems), clozapine is generally not recommended while breastfeeding. If used, the baby should be monitored very closely by pediatrics.
sections.pediatrics: Clozapine is used in children and adolescents only for severe, treatment-resistant schizophrenia and usually under specialist care. Dosing is weight-based and titrated slowly. Children may be at higher risk of some side effects (eg, metabolic problems, movement symptoms), and they still require full ANC monitoring.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are more sensitive to clozapine’s side effects—especially low blood pressure, sedation, falls, constipation, confusion, and heart issues. Start at very low doses, increase very slowly, and use the smallest effective dose. Antipsychotics in general are associated with increased stroke and mortality risk in older adults with dementia.
sections.hepatic: Liver disease can increase clozapine levels. Use lower starting doses, slower titration, and regular monitoring of liver tests. Stop and evaluate if there are signs of liver injury (jaundice, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant pain).
sections.renal: Kidney impairment may increase clozapine exposure. Start at low doses, titrate slowly, and monitor for side effects. Dose reductions may be needed in significant kidney impairment.
sections.smokers: Cigarette smoking lowers clozapine levels; smokers often need higher doses. Stopping smoking can raise levels and cause toxicity if the dose is not reduced. Plan ahead for hospitalizations or smoke-free settings.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Absolute neutrophil count (ANC): Mandatory baseline and ongoing ANC monitoring (typically weekly for 6 months, then every 2 weeks for 6 months, then monthly if stable). Different thresholds apply for people with Duffy-null associated neutrophil counts.
Vital signs: Blood pressure (including orthostatic), heart rate, temperature at baseline and regularly—especially in the first few weeks and after dose increases.

Myocarditis/cardiomyopathy monitoring: Watch for chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, fatigue, unexplained fever, and resting tachycardia. Some clinicians monitor CRP and troponin weekly for the first 4–6 weeks.
Metabolic monitoring: Weight/BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and lipid panel at baseline, around 3–4 months after starting, then at least annually (more often if abnormal).
Bowel function: Ask about bowel movements at every visit; track frequency, consistency, and associated symptoms. Consider prophylactic laxatives.
Liver and kidney function: Periodic liver enzymes and renal function tests, especially in those with preexisting disease or on other hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic drugs.
Neurologic status: Monitor for seizures, myoclonus, confusion, delirium, or new movement symptoms. Consider EEG if clinically indicated or at higher doses.
ECG: Baseline in those with cardiac risk factors or on other QT-prolonging drugs; repeat if symptoms occur or if risk factors change.
Adherence and side effects: At every visit, assess how consistently clozapine is taken, barriers to adherence (labs, side effects, logistics), and emerging adverse effects.
Smoking status and drug interactions: Regularly review tobacco use and new medications to anticipate changes in clozapine levels and risks.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Several clozapine formulations are available to help with swallowing issues and dose flexibility. All require enrollment in a monitoring program for blood counts.
items: Tablets (Clozaril and generics): 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg.
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT, generics): 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 150 mg, 200 mg (dissolve on the tongue; helpful if swallowing tablets is difficult).
Oral suspension (Versacloz): 50 mg/mL (use included oral syringes; shake well before use).
Scored strengths (some generics): Allow smaller dose adjustments when titrating.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Clozapine works differently from most other antipsychotics. It blocks dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, but binds relatively loosely to D2 compared with other drugs. It also affects many other receptors (dopamine, serotonin, adrenergic, muscarinic, histamine). This broad activity seems to help with treatment-resistant psychosis and suicidality, but it also causes many of clozapine’s side effects—like sedation (histamine), weight gain and metabolic changes (serotonin and histamine), drooling and constipation (muscarinic and gut serotonin effects), and low blood pressure (alpha-1 adrenergic blockade).

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text:
Clozapine is not a first-line antipsychotic. It comes into play after at least two adequate trials of other antipsychotics (at correct doses and durations) have failed. At that point, continuing to cycle through more of the same treatments yields diminishing returns and ongoing risk of disability and suicide. Clozapine offers a unique chance of meaningful recovery for many of these individuals.

Because of its serious risks and monitoring requirements, clozapine is usually prescribed and managed by psychiatrists with experience in its use, often in coordination with primary care or specialty clinics for metabolic and cardiovascular monitoring. Once a person responds and tolerates it, clozapine is generally continued long-term, with ongoing ANC monitoring and close attention to metabolic health and bowel function.

faqs.a: Clozapine is used mainly for treatment-resistant schizophrenia—when at least two other antipsychotics have not provided enough benefit. It is also approved to reduce the risk of suicidal behavior in people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who are at ongoing risk. Because of serious side effects, it is reserved for situations where the potential benefits clearly outweigh the risks.

faqs.q: Why does clozapine require regular blood tests?
faqs.a: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia—a dangerous drop in neutrophils, a type of white blood cell needed to fight infections. This can lead to life-threatening infections. To reduce this risk, you must have regular blood tests (ANC checks) before starting and throughout treatment. If your neutrophil count drops too low, clozapine must be stopped or paused, and your team will decide if and when it can be restarted.

faqs.q: How long does clozapine take to work?
faqs.a: Clozapine is titrated slowly to reduce side effects, so it doesn’t work overnight. Some people notice early changes within 1–2 weeks, but meaningful improvements in hallucinations, paranoia, mood, and functioning usually build over 4–8 weeks or longer. Clozapine is generally considered a long-term treatment once it’s working well.

faqs.q: What are the most serious side effects of clozapine?
faqs.a: The most serious risks are severe neutropenia (dangerously low white blood cells), myocarditis and cardiomyopathy (life-threatening heart inflammation or damage), seizures, severe constipation and bowel blockage, blood clots, and metabolic problems (weight gain, diabetes, high cholesterol). Fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, or signs of infection on clozapine are medical red flags and should be evaluated urgently.

Yes. Clozapine is one of the antipsychotics most strongly associated with weight gain, increased appetite, and metabolic changes like high cholesterol and diabetes. Weight often increases rapidly after starting, then continues to rise more slowly over time. Lifestyle measures (diet, exercise, sleep) and regular lab checks are important, and sometimes additional medications are needed to manage metabolic effects.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking clozapine?
faqs.a: It’s best to avoid alcohol on clozapine. Both clozapine and alcohol can cause sedation, dizziness, confusion, and low blood pressure. Together they increase the risk of falls, accidents, and breathing problems. Alcohol can also make it harder to notice warning signs of serious side effects or infections.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a dose of clozapine?
faqs.a: If you miss a single dose, take it as soon as you remember that same day unless it is almost time for your next dose. Do not double up. If you miss clozapine for more than 48 hours, you must NOT restart at your previous dose—you’ll need to restart at 12.5 mg and retitrate under your prescriber’s guidance to reduce the risk of severe low blood pressure and heart problems.

faqs.q: What signs of infection should I watch for on clozapine?
faqs.a: Call your doctor or seek urgent care if you develop fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, flu-like symptoms, extreme fatigue, shortness of breath, or any sign of a serious infection. These could be early signs of neutropenia or pneumonia. Do not wait for your next routine blood draw if you feel acutely unwell.

Data are limited and mixed. Clozapine can be used in pregnancy when the benefits clearly outweigh the risks—for example, in someone with severe, treatment-resistant illness who becomes stable on clozapine before pregnancy. All antipsychotics in late pregnancy can cause withdrawal or movement symptoms in newborns. Clozapine also increases the risk of diabetes and weight gain in the pregnant parent. Decisions about continuing or stopping clozapine in pregnancy should involve both psychiatry and obstetrics and use shared decision-making.

faqs.q: Can I breastfeed while taking clozapine?
faqs.a: Clozapine enters breast milk and has been associated with sedation and at least one case of suspected agranulocytosis in a breastfed infant. Because of these risks, most guidelines recommend avoiding breastfeeding while on clozapine. If breastfeeding is considered despite the risks, the baby should be closely monitored by a pediatrician for sedation, feeding problems, and blood count changes.

faqs.q: What does smoking have to do with clozapine?
faqs.a: Cigarette smoke speeds up the breakdown of clozapine in the liver, lowering its level in your blood. Smokers usually need higher clozapine doses than non-smokers. If you stop smoking, clozapine levels can rise sharply, increasing the risk of side effects like seizures or severe sedation unless your dose is reduced. Always tell your prescriber if you change your smoking habits.

For many people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, the answer is yes—clozapine may be the only medication that gives them real relief from severe psychosis or suicidality. But it is not the right choice for everyone. The decision involves balancing potential life-changing benefits against serious risks and the burden of ongoing blood tests and monitoring. This decision should be made with a psychiatrist who knows your history, ideally with input from family or supports if you’re comfortable with that.
